learn.intro: The Spinning Jenny, the Water Frame, the power loom and the steam engine moved work from homes into factories, and people from villages into fast-growing cities. Did machines change lives more than anything else? And did industrialisation transform life for everyone?

sections.title: 1. From hand to machine

ul: James Hargreaves' Spinning Jenny (in use from the mid-1760s, patented 1770) let one worker spin several threads at once.
Richard Arkwright's Water Frame (1769) used water power to spin stronger thread. It needed a mill by a river: Cromford Mill (1771) was one of the first true factories.
Edmund Cartwright's power loom (1785) mechanised weaving, but was unreliable at first and took decades to spread: mechanisation was gradual.
James Watt's improved steam engine (patented 1769, refined in the 1770s–80s) freed factories from rivers, so industry grew in coalfield towns.

blocks.p: The factory system mattered as much as the machines. Under the "domestic" or "putting-out" system, people worked at home at their own pace. In factories, machines, clocks, bells and fines set the pace. Some workers earned more, but many lost control over their working lives.

evidence: Water Frame 1769; Cromford Mill 1771; power loom 1785.

blocks.p: Manchester grew from around 18,000 people in the 1750s to over 300,000 by 1850, driven by cotton.
Push factors (low farm wages, loss of common land after enclosure) and pull factors (factory jobs, often higher wages) drove migration to towns.
Growth was unplanned. Working-class families often lived in overcrowded back-to-back houses, sharing an outdoor toilet with many others, with no running water or rubbish removal.

Experience depended on class. Middle-class factory owners, merchants and professionals lived in larger homes, enjoyed new shops, theatres and parks, and sometimes moved to suburbs away from pollution. There was no single experience of "the industrial city".

timeline.event: Hargreaves' Spinning Jenny comes into use.
Arkwright's Water Frame; Watt patents his steam engine.

misconceptions.right: The power loom took decades to be widely used.

misconceptions.wrong: Factories made every worker better off.
misconceptions.right: Some earned more, but many lost control of their time and pace of work.

misconceptions.wrong: Everyone in industrial cities lived in slums.

sources.title: Cromford Mill, Derbyshire
sources.origin: Built by Richard Arkwright; now part of the Derwent Valley Mills World Heritage Site.
sources.usefulness: Shows how factories were organised around power and machines. A building alone cannot tell us how workers felt.

mcq.q: What did the Spinning Jenny allow?
options: One worker to spin several threads at once

mcq.q: Why did the Water Frame lead to factories?
options: It was small enough for homes
It needed water power, so it was housed in mills by rivers
It was invented in a city

mcq.q: What did Watt's steam engine change?
options: Factories no longer had to be by fast rivers

mcq.q: What does the slow spread of the power loom show?
Which is a PULL factor for moving to towns?

options: They lived in the same housing
Larger homes, new leisure, sometimes suburbs

What word means the growth of towns and cities?

matching.title: Push or pull?
pairs: Push: lost rights in the village

evidence.q: Explain how the factory system changed the experience of work.
evidence.model: Under the domestic system people worked at home at their own pace; in factories, machines, clocks, bells and fines set the pace, so workers lost control over their time.

evidence.q: Give precise evidence that urbanisation was rapid but affected classes differently.
evidence.model: Manchester grew from about 18,000 in the 1750s to over 300,000 by 1850; working-class families crowded into back-to-backs while middle-class families had larger homes and moved to suburbs.

sources.label: Source A
sources.provenance: Cromford Mill, Derbyshire, opened by Richard Arkwright in 1771. It is now part of the Derwent Valley Mills World Heritage Site.
sources.text: A tall stone mill of several storeys beside a fast-flowing stream, with a water wheel to drive the machines. The windows are large to let in light for long shifts. Arkwright also built rows of cottages, a chapel and a market nearby for the workers and their families, many of them children.

questions.sources_note: Source A is described in our own words for revision practice. In the exam you will be given the source itself.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: "Machines changed people's lives more than anything else during the Industrial Revolution." How far do you agree?
questions.asks: Weigh machines against the factory system and urbanisation, using the four criteria.
steps: Explain the impact of machines with evidence.
Explain another change (factory system or urbanisation).
Use at least two criteria to judge.
questions.plan: 3 minutes planning, 11 minutes writing, 1 minute checking.

full: P: Machines changed lives to a large / some extent, but…
E: For example, the Water Frame (1769)…
E: In terms of depth / scale, this meant that… However, urbanisation…
J: Therefore, the biggest change was…
some: P – Topic sentence with a qualifier (blue): One key reason … / To a large extent … / On the other hand …
E – Precisely selected evidence (purple), in order with time connectives (green): At the start … / Later … / Eventually … / Finally …
E – Explain with arguing connectives (red): However … / This was more important because … / In contrast …
J – Judgement: This shows that … / Overall, the most important reason was … / Therefore, I agree to a large/limited extent …
